name: Respiratory Quotient Calculator
seoDesc: The respiratory quotient is carbon dioxide produced divided by oxygen consumed. Free respiratory quotient calculator: enter your values and get respiratory qu
summary:
The respiratory quotient is carbon dioxide produced divided by oxygen consumed. It returns respiratory quotient, non-protein RQ, energy equivalent and fat share of fuel, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It identifies which fuel a tissue is burning — 1.0 for carbohydrate, 0.7 for fat, 0.8 for protein — and it is the link between gas exchange and energy expenditure. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Respiratory Quotient
sections.html:
RQ = VCO₂ ÷ VO₂

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
VCO₂carbon dioxide producedmL/min
VO₂oxygen consumedmL/min
RQrespiratory quotient—

sections.title: How do I use the Respiratory Quotient?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: co₂ produced of 200 mL/min, o₂ consumed of 250 mL/min.

Substituting them into the formula gives respiratory quotient of 0.8, non-protein rq of 0.8, energy equivalent of 4.04 kcal/L O₂, fat share of fuel of 66.67%.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
0.7Fatalmost pure lipid oxidation
0.8Protein / mixedtypical of a mixed diet at rest
1.0Carbohydratepure glucose oxidation
above 1.0Not oxidationlipogenesis or hyperventilation — check the measurement

  • An RQ above 1.0 cannot come from burning a fuel: it appears during lipogenesis, when CO₂ is produced without corresponding O₂ use, or when the subject hyperventilates.

  • The energy equivalent rises with RQ, from 4.69 kcal per litre of O₂ for fat to 5.05 for carbohydrate, which is why indirect calorimetry needs the RQ.

  • For whole-body measurements the value is usually called the respiratory exchange ratio (RER) and includes protein oxidation.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Using RQ from a spirometry session where the subject was breathing hard.
  • Assuming 0.82 is always right for a resting subject.
  • Mixing volumes in litres and millilitres between the two boxes.

faq.q: Why is RQ higher on a high-carbohydrate diet?
faq.a: Because carbohydrate oxidation releases more CO₂ per O₂ consumed than fat does.

faq.q: What does the Respiratory Quotient actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns respiratory quotient, non-protein RQ, energy equivalent and fat share of fuel. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
